podcast.body: A song from their 2004 album "Elephant," which is speculated to have been the single most played indie rock song of the 2000s, contributing significantly to the album's monster success. "The white stripes and seven-ation army from their 2004 album Elephant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The iconic seven-note riff was played on a late 1950s/early 1960s K Archtop guitar. Its bass-like sound was achieved by funneling it through a whammy pedal set to transpose the sound down one octave, and it was amplified by a mid-1960s Sears department store amplifier. "The 7 note riff was played on that K Archtop. And the reason it sounds like a bass guitar is because it's funneled through a whammy pedal set to transpose the sound down one octave."

podcast.body: The leading track from the "Elephant" album, this song is a primitive and simple rock hit distinguished by a guitar riff (often mistaken for a bass) that became instantly recognizable and deeply embedded in popular culture. Its 4x4 drum beat was noted for its similarity to Detroit techno, and the song evolved into a global phenomenon, frequently heard at football matches and events worldwide. "Sí, aunque suene como un bajo es una guitarra."

srcs.episode: Por qué White Stripes desaparecieron en su mejor momento?

podcast.body: The riff for this song, featuring many different colors of distortion, was created by running an early 1960s K Hollow Body guitar, equipped with a single pickup, into a Digitech Whammy pedal, which shifted the notes Jack White played down an entire octave. Jack White later played the same seven notes on the same guitar with a slide, without pitch shifting, but run through a Big Muff Pi effects pedal with the sustain turned almost all the way up. The signal then went to a Sears Silver Tone amplifier from the mid-1960s, set with a little extra bass and treble, resulting in awesome distorted tones. "The riff was created by running a K Hollow Body guitar from the early 1960s, equipped with a single pickup into a Digitech whammy pedal, which shifted the notes Jack White played down an entire octave."

podcast.body: The song's distinctive seven-note riff originated from Jack White during a soundcheck at the Corner Hotel in Melbourne, Australia, on January 29, 2002. Initially, it was met with skepticism by Ben Swank of Third Man Records, and Jack White briefly entertained the idea of it becoming a James Bond theme. A year later, it was developed further at Toe Rags, a primitive analog studio in England, beginning as a "little experiment" without a complete chorus or lyrics. The song was eventually completed, retaining its working title, and upon its release as a single from the "Elephant" album, it achieved massive radio success, critical acclaim, and a popular video. It won a Grammy for Best Rock Song and was nominated for Best Rock Performance, ultimately becoming the band's most popular song, a global sports anthem, and adopted by political movements in the UK and Israel. "It then won a Grammy for Best Rock song and was also nominated for Best Rock Performance."
